summary: For ages 5–7, help children apply one child-usable rule to tell real dinosaurs apart from commonly confused prehistoric creatures (flying pterosaurs, swimming plesiosaurs, sail-backed Dimetrodon), and to recognise that movie/cartoon dinosaurs are not always accurate. The rule to teach: a dinosaur was a land animal whose legs went straight DOWN underneath its body; flyers and swimmers are 'cousins' that lived at the same time, not dinosaurs. A second strand builds early media literacy: compare a screen dinosaur to current science (feathers, size, sounds, and whether humans appear alongside it) to see that confident-looking pictures aren't always right, and that some details (exact sound and colour) simply aren't known from bones. Keep it playful and non-punitive — near-misses are chances to re-apply the rule.
misconceptions: 'Pterodactyls/pterosaurs are flying dinosaurs' — they are flying reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Plesiosaurs (and other big sea reptiles) are dinosaurs' — they are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Dimetrodon (the sail-back) is a dinosaur' — it lived before dinosaurs and is not one.
'Movie dinosaurs show exactly what they looked like' — films exaggerate size, sounds, and often omit feathers.
'If it's big, extinct, and scaly, it's a dinosaur' — being extinct or reptile-like doesn't make an animal a dinosaur.

activities.title: Dinosaur Club bouncer: sort with a clue lens
steps: Act as a 'bouncer' at the Dinosaur Club where only real dinosaurs get in; creatures line up one at a time: T. rex, Triceratops, a leathery-winged pterosaur, a long-necked flippered plesiosaur, and a sail-backed Dimetrodon.
For each creature, decide DINOSAUR or NOT-A-DINOSAUR and place it in that bin.
Use a 'clue lens' that highlights the deciding feature — legs straight down under the body (dinosaur), or leathery wings, flippers, or legs sprawling out to the sides (not a dinosaur).
Say or tap the reason out loud, e.g. 'wings — a flying reptile, a cousin, not a dinosaur.'
activities.insight: Being scary, scaly, big, or extinct does NOT make an animal a dinosaur — there is a simple rule (land animal, legs straight underneath) that you can apply yourself to decide.

activities.title: Movie vs real: spot what the film got wrong or guessed
steps: Look at an exaggerated screen/cartoon dinosaur beside a 'best-science' version of the same animal.

Point to the things the film clearly got wrong: the wrong size, humans shown living alongside the dinosaur, and — where the best-science version of this animal has feathers — a bare scaly skin that leaves those feathers out.
Then point to the things the film shows as if certain but that we can't actually know from bones — the exact loud roar and the exact skin colour.
Name one difference out loud, e.g. 'the real one may have had feathers', 'people never lived with giant dinosaurs like this one', or 'we don't actually know the sound it made.'
activities.insight: A confident-looking picture on a screen isn't always what the science says: films exaggerate size, often leave out feathers, and sometimes show people with dinosaurs who never actually lived together, while some details (exact colour, exact sound) simply aren't known from bones, so showing them as certain is a guess dressed up as fact.

activities.title: Land / air / sea cousins gallery (scaffold)
steps: Explore a labelled scene with three cousins: a dinosaur on land, a pterosaur in the air, a plesiosaur in the sea.
Tap each creature to reveal 'dinosaur / not a dinosaur — because…' with the deciding feature named.
Open a flap that contrasts a movie dinosaur with a real one.
activities.insight: Dinosaurs, flying reptiles, and sea reptiles are different groups that lived at the same time; flyers and swimmers are important, real cousins — not dinosaurs, and not 'fake'.

activities.title: Ask the palaeontologist (alternative)
steps: Pose 'is this a dinosaur?' questions to a palaeontologist character — e.g. 'Is a pterodactyl a dinosaur?' or 'Is the movie right about the roar?'
Listen to the gentle correction and then restate the rule in your own words.
Try a follow-up: give the character one creature and predict what they'll say before they answer.
activities.insight: An expert uses the same simple rule you can use — flyers and swimmers are cousins, not dinosaurs — and separates known bone evidence from guesses about sound and colour.

activities.title: Quick check: which is NOT a dinosaur? (light assessment)
steps: Sort a small set of creatures into dinosaur / not-a-dinosaur.
Answer 'which of these is NOT a dinosaur?' and give the reason.
Answer 'name one thing a movie might get wrong about a dinosaur.'
activities.insight: You can state that pterosaurs flew but were not dinosaurs, that plesiosaurs swam but were not dinosaurs, and name at least one way a movie dinosaur differs from the real animal.

checkQuestion: A picture book shows a flying reptile (a pterosaur like Pteranodon) and a long-necked sea reptile (a plesiosaur) and calls them both 'dinosaurs'. Is the book right? And in a movie, the dinosaurs roar loudly and have dry scaly skin — is that definitely how the real ones were? Explain.
checkAnswer: The book is wrong: pterosaurs (flying) and plesiosaurs (swimming) lived at the same time as dinosaurs but were NOT dinosaurs — dinosaurs were a particular family of mostly land animals. And movies aren't always accurate: we don't actually know the sounds dinosaurs made or their exact skin and colour, and many had feathers — so a roaring, scaly movie dinosaur may not match the real animal.
